0c929c2e13da8b88e97b65d9f4ffa0af7a008455.en: The 1990s in Ukraine were a time of instability, material deprivation and complex relationships between parents and children. Against this backdrop unfolds the touching friendship between little Timofey, a sensitive boy who grew up without a father’s care, and Felix – his grandmother’s eccentric friend, a veteran of the war in Afghanistan. Felix suffers from post-traumatic stress and finds solace in music and alcohol. ‘Rock. Paper. Hand grenade’ is a raw, yet tender and heart-warming coming-of-age story about the first lessons in kindness and cruelty, teenage love, and the role of family and friends in the unstable environment of post-Soviet Ukraine. Irina Tsilik’s feature film debut is a moving coming-of-age drama set against the backdrop of the 1990s. (And of an inscrutable future that turned out to be harsher and darker.) Irina co-wrote the screenplay for *Stone. Paper. Grenade* with her husband Artem Chekh, author of the novel *Who Are You?*. Chekh is currently serving in the Ukrainian army. His book, which inspired the film, is a biography of a real-life figure of whom he has fond memories. The film’s wonderfully melancholic pace is down to the director’s masterful handling of sound and music. Every scene is carefully thought out and calibrated. Three different actors – Andriy Cherednyk, Vladyslav Balyuk and Volodymyr Hladkyi – take on the role of Tymofii at different ages. The role of his mother is played by the talented Anastasia Karpenko, known for her brilliant performance in the film *How Is Katya?*. Ukrainian director and journalist Iryna Tsilik made a name for herself with the documentary *The Earth Is Blue Like an Orange* (2020), which won the competition at Sundance in 2020; and was selected for the Berlinale, IDFA and more than 100 other international festivals.

4769be8d7ae26222e68a983a3eb0362fcd83ad85.en: Fifteen stab wounds in 27 seconds. This is what Salman Rushdie went through before opening his only functioning eye and looking at the camera. Together with his wife, Rachel Eliza Griffiths, the writer decided to document his slow return to life a few days after the brutal attack in New York. Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney unfolds a painful and deeply insightful story that traces Salman Rushdie’s rehabilitation and pays tribute to his indomitable spirit, humour and optimism. The story begins following the publication of *The Satanic Verses*, when a religious edict, a ‘fatwa’, was issued against Rushdie by the Iranian Ayatollah Khomeini. From that moment on, the writer lived under constant threat for decades, fighting for the right to free public expression. The culmination of the persecution is captured in a harrowing recording of the assassination attempt… Rushdie will return to the scene of the crime to bring this dark chapter of his life to a close, but is that even possible? A powerfully resonant documentary narrative that explores the themes of religion and art as an explosive combination. Salman Rushdie, a brilliant writer and intellectual with a cosmopolitan spirit, reflects on violence, forgiveness and the right to free speech – themes that are more relevant than ever.

47837d59e5b2585b7b1019f8b78b6e18d111e0eb.en: Nora, Thomas and their daughter Ida live peacefully on a secluded farm. Their only neighbour is the Italian artist Cristina (Monica Bellucci). Whilst everyone is preparing for a surprise party to celebrate Nora’s birthday, three suspicious men begin loitering around the house. Before long, they take it upon themselves to join the celebrations. Tranquillity gives way to anxiety and tension. The film is an adaptation of the noir novel of the same name by Laurent Mouvignier – a skilfully layered socio-psychological narrative structured as a crime thriller. The author puts forward the idea that dangers and anxieties do not strike suddenly, but slowly seep into everyday life. As the characters’ pasts come to light, it turns out that almost every one of them bears the burden of some form of remorse, fear, past humiliation or unresolved trauma. 82f1aef11401bd4c8326782cf921d0b65eb5c7f3.en: The film focuses on the lives of Jean and Corinne Lucher – a father and daughter in occupied France. She is a young film star, whilst he is a powerful media magnate and a friend of Otto Abetz, the influential Nazi ambassador in Paris. The story is told from the perspective of Corinne, once hailed as ‘the new Garbo’. As she records her thoughts on a borrowed tape recorder, she tries to reconcile her unwavering love for her father with the fact that he was executed for treason in 1946. Despite its impressive running time of over three hours, *Lights and Shadows* attracted more than 300,000 cinema-goers in France in the first week after its release alone. The film also sparked a heated debate regarding the Vichy regime. Whilst many critics from the centre and the right praised it as a masterpiece that captures the historical nuances, left-wing publications such as L’Humanité have criticised it for downplaying the actions of those who voluntarily served the Nazi killing machine right to the very end. Laurent Joly – a leading French historian specialising in the Vichy regime and state anti-Semitism – has praised the film for its ‘ambiguity’ and ‘duplicity’. According to Joly, “it was not pacifism that drove Luchère towards collaboration, but his venality and lack of morals”. ‘Light and Shadow’ is a harrowing reflection on moral compromises, cruelty, valour and all that remains in our lives against the backdrop of major historical upheavals. Rather than overwhelming the viewer with raw emotion, Xavier Giannoli unfolds the story with patience and delicacy. Silence is part of the narrative language, whilst the contrast between light and shadow serves as a subtle metaphor for memory, absence and the fragile resilience of human bonds. The cinematography in *Rays and Shadows* is never an end in itself or merely decorative – it serves the film’s emotional core. The actors’ performances are restrained and precise, devoid of theatricality. Every gesture feels authentic and dramaturgically justified. If you’re looking for a conventional plot or instant gratification, this isn’t the film for you. But if you’re ready for something more contemplative and introspective – something that resonates rather than forcing its message upon you – *Rays and Shadows* will offer you an exceptionally rewarding experience. A film of rare sensitivity, in which the invisible is just as important as the visible. (anonymous viewer review)

dd09c423ea5bfbd919b655409889453d5286d861.en: Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira), the director of a care home for the elderly, is keen to introduce an innovative approach to institutional care, despite the reluctance of some of the staff. Based on a philosophy of empathy and mindful presence, the Humanitude approach involves listening to and respecting the personal dignity of each resident. On the verge of physical and mental exhaustion, Marie-Lou decides to attend a theatre performance to which she has been invited by chance, after helping a young boy she does not know. After the performance, she meets the Japanese director Marie (Tao Okamoto). An extraordinary friendship blossoms between the two women, bound by the idealistic aspiration ‘to make the impossible possible’. The film is a loose adaptation of the documentary book of letters *When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn*, co-written by Maoko Miyano and Maho Isono. The book bears witness to their warm friendship and mutual support. Ryusuke Hamaguchi transports this tender, intellectually stimulating and humane story to the Parisian suburbs. With his first film made outside Japan, the director demonstrates his unique gift for employing subtle emotional nuances and balancing dialogue with silence. The plot unfolds patiently, with an exceptional sensitivity to every gesture, allowing the conversations and silences to generate profound emotional power.

The concert was part of the famous Magic Tour – the last tour on which the band travelled the world with their lead singer, Freddie Mercury. Three years before the fall of the Berlin Wall, this was the first concert by a Western rock band to be held in a stadium behind the Iron Curtain. ec0454dcc1d5cfdcc5a46f4f874af8192e575b72.en: Young Violette Tréne is the caretaker of the cemetery in a small town in Burgundy. A job that many would find off-putting, but for her compassionate heart it is a salvation and a refuge. In this oasis of silence, free from the hustle and bustle of everyday life, Violette has developed a knack for savouring the little things: tending to the flowers, a fragrant cup of tea, freshly picked fruit. Her tranquillity is disrupted by the sudden appearance of a mysterious man who attempts to unearth long-buried secrets. In turn, Violet is forced to confront her past in order to give life and love a new chance. Director Jean-Pierre Jeunet, winner of dozens of awards and honours for iconic films such as *The Unbelievable Fate of Amélie Poulain* (a César for Best Film and Best Director, a BAFTA for Best Screenplay, an Oscar nomination, and more), *The Longest Engagement*, ‘Delicacy’ and ‘The City of Lost Children’, returns with a new cinematic gem, a life-affirming tale and a feast for the senses – an apotheosis of humanity, delicacy and beauty. The film is a masterful adaptation of the international bestseller *Water for the Flowers* by Valérie Perrin, translated into over 30 languages and selling more than a million copies worldwide. The book has won numerous awards, including the prestigious ‘Maison de la Presse’ prize. ‘Water for the Flowers’ was also the best-selling book in Italy in 2020.

ec924723d56c437e112c03b027f817f76f981814.en: An insightful portrait of the American novelist and essayist Siri Hustvedt: her literary evolution, her relationship with Paul Auster, and her reflections on feminism and the philosophy of our times. Rather than following the logic of a chronological biography, the film explores the ideas and personal experiences that have shaped Hustvedt’s views and underpin her work. The film traces Siri Hustvedt’s life from her childhood in Minnesota to her move to New York, where she became one of the leading voices in contemporary American literature. Her reflections on literature, identity, memory, neuroscience, psychoanalysis, feminism and the creative process are interwoven with scenes from her daily life and landmark interviews. A central theme of the film is her long-standing partnership with the irreplaceable American writer Paul Auster. Whilst filming was underway – a process that lasted several years – Auster received a serious diagnosis. Thus, the film, which begins as a portrait of a writer’s intellectual life, gradually evolves into an intimate and moving reflection on love, illness, vulnerability and grief. Many critics note that this emotional shift lends the film’s narrative a powerful resonance and depth. The title is metaphorical. It suggests that the ‘self’ cannot be clearly captured or defined. One approaches it indirectly – through memory, language, relationships, art and the body. This image is largely consistent with Hustvet’s work, which repeatedly questions the stability of identity and emphasises that consciousness is fluid and relative.

f18d5153902340b07e5739f1dffd937cbdf7dbe6.en: 1943. In the heart of the jungle, in a Japanese prisoner-of-war camp situated along the Thailand – Burma, Lieutenant-Colonel Dorigo Evans is tormented by the memory of a far too brief but fateful love affair – the one with his uncle’s wife, Amy Mulvaney. It is precisely this memory that becomes his inner anchor as he struggles to cling to life amidst the endless shadow of death. The love between Dorigo and Amy blossomed years earlier – from the moment they first met, she never left his thoughts, despite his long-standing marriage to Ella Evans, his secret affair with Lynette Maison and his life-changing friendship with the soldier Frank Gardner. An adaptation of the novel of the same name by Richard Flanagan, winner of the Man Booker Prize, ‘The Narrow Road to the Deep North’ is a multi-layered narrative: a timeless love story, an intimate exploration of character, a clash of cultures seen from both sides of the conflict, and an honest look at a long-standing partnership. The series *The Narrow Road to the Deep North* is produced by the Australian company Curio Pictures, with the support of Sony Pictures Television. Sean Grant is the screenwriter and executive producer, whilst Justin Kurzel is the director and also an executive producer. The screenplay adaptation is the result of a collaboration between screenwriter Sean Grant and Richard Flanagan himself.
